quotes.text: Facts are the measurements how many, how much, how often? Dimensions are the descriptions, the who, what, when and where.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Crisp definition of the fact versus dimension split at the heart of star schema design.

quotes.text: If you want a mental image, facts are the receipts. Dimensions are the catalog. Receipts don't carry full product names, addresses, or job titles. They just reference IDs and amounts
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Memorable analogy that makes dimensional modeling easy to grasp.

quotes.text: Pick a grain and stick to it. Grain is the detail level of your fact per transaction, per order line, or per daily roll up. Mixing grains in one table is like throwing metric and imperial units together.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear, practical modeling rule with an intuitive comparison.

quotes.text: A date table isn't glamorous, but it's the backbone of every reliable report. Skip it, and no amount of clever measures will save you.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Strong recommendation on why a dedicated date table is non-negotiable.

chapters.title: From digital spaghetti to a star schema
Normalize the fact, flatten the dimension
Beating blanks, flags and cryptic codes

takeaways: A single flat table forces Power BI's engine to scan duplicated text on every query, while a star schema with slim fact tables and descriptive dimension tables keeps filters fast and correct.
Normalize facts with surrogate keys and a single grain, and flatten dimensions instead of building snowflake chains.
A dedicated date table with role-playing copies, plus cleaned-up blanks, flags and codes in Power Query, makes time intelligence reliable and slicers trustworthy.
hook: Is your Power BI report crawling every time someone adds a filter? This episode is for report authors and data modelers fighting tangled tables and fragile DAX. Learn how a clean star schema, a proper date table and human-readable slicers make models fast and trustworthy.
